item.title: Alibaba denies Qwen post-training chief’s departure, plans lawsuit over rumor
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Alibaba’s Qwen team denied on Friday that its post-training chief Zhou Hao had left the company and said it would sue the online publisher behind the claim. The response followed an article by the account “Top Huaren Kechuang She,” which alleged his departure. Qwen said the article fabricated the personnel change and even used the […]
item.content:encoded:
Alibaba’s Qwen team denied on Friday that its post-training chief Zhou Hao had left the company and said it would sue the online publisher behind the claim. The response followed an article by the account “Top Huaren Kechuang She,” which alleged his departure. Qwen said the article fabricated the personnel change and even used the wrong Chinese character in Zhou’s name.

Zhou previously worked on AI research at Meta and Google DeepMind. Google’s Gemini 1.0 technical report listed him as a co-lead of work on factual accuracy in Gemini applications. Earlier reports said he joined Alibaba in January 2026 and subsequently moved to its Tongyi laboratory to oversee Qwen’s post-training work.

Post-training is the stage used to refine a pretrained model’s instruction following, reasoning and behavior for practical applications. Qwen said inaccurate claims about its model team have appeared repeatedly and that it would pursue legal action against those responsible. [MyDrivers, in Chinese]

item.title: Mercedes launches hybrid CLA in China with Doubao AI and Momenta driving system
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Mercedes-Benz launched its new hybrid CLA at the Guangzhou Auto Show on Friday, with introductory prices ranging from RMB199,000 to RMB245,600. The two versions have official list prices of RMB229,000 and RMB285,600. The model combines a 48V hybrid powertrain with Chinese-developed AI services for the cabin and driver assistance. Built on Mercedes’ MB.OS software architecture, […]
item.content:encoded:
Mercedes-Benz launched its new hybrid CLA at the Guangzhou Auto Show on Friday, with introductory prices ranging from RMB199,000 to RMB245,600. The two versions have official list prices of RMB229,000 and RMB285,600. The model combines a 48V hybrid powertrain with Chinese-developed AI services for the cabin and driver assistance.

Built on Mercedes’ MB.OS software architecture, the CLA uses a city and highway navigation-assisted driving system jointly developed with Momenta. The system is based on Momenta’s R7 world model and supports parking-space-to-parking-space assistance. Its virtual assistant incorporates ByteDance’s Doubao AI model, enabling multi-command interactions and emotion recognition, while vehicle software can receive over-the-air updates.

The powertrain combines an M252 four-cylinder turbocharged engine, an electrified eight-speed dual-clutch transmission and a 48V lithium battery. The transmission-integrated electric motor produces up to 22kW and 200Nm, supporting electric coasting. Mercedes quotes combined fuel consumption as low as 4.91 liters per 100km. The car retains the electric CLA’s coupe-style profile, frameless doors and illuminated star-pattern grille. [IT Home, in Chinese]

item.title: Xiaomi reportedly plans December launch for second-generation AI glasses, including display version
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Xiaomi plans to launch its second-generation AI glasses in mid-December alongside the standard Xiaomi 18 smartphone, with sales expected to begin the same day, according to a report published Friday. The lineup reportedly includes a Q95 Pro model, an electrochromic-lens version with four tint settings, and a version equipped with a display. A display-equipped model […]
item.content:encoded:
Xiaomi plans to launch its second-generation AI glasses in mid-December alongside the standard Xiaomi 18 smartphone, with sales expected to begin the same day, according to a report published Friday. The lineup reportedly includes a Q95 Pro model, an electrochromic-lens version with four tint settings, and a version equipped with a display.

A display-equipped model would expand Xiaomi’s glasses beyond the camera-and-audio format of its first generation. The original product, introduced in June last year at a starting price of RMB1,999, weighs 40 grams and combines a 12-megapixel camera with open-ear speakers and a five-microphone system.

The first-generation glasses support first-person photography and video recording, with third-party apps enabling video calls and livestreaming. The reported second-generation lineup would add more hardware choices, particularly for users seeking visual information in the glasses themselves. Xiaomi has not announced specifications or pricing for the new models. [STAR Market Daily, in Chinese]

item.title: Tencent launches Hy3D 3.6 for professional 3D asset generation
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Tencent released Hy3D 3.6 on Friday, upgrading its 3D generation model with more detailed geometry and improved physically based rendering materials. The model is available through Tencent Cloud’s Token Hub API and has been integrated into the company’s Miora creative agent, LAP game-asset platform and WorkRally filmmaking platform. Hy3D 3.6 learns the geometry, textures and […]
item.content:encoded:
Tencent released Hy3D 3.6 on Friday, upgrading its 3D generation model with more detailed geometry and improved physically based rendering materials. The model is available through Tencent Cloud’s Token Hub API and has been integrated into the company’s Miora creative agent, LAP game-asset platform and WorkRally filmmaking platform.

Hy3D 3.6 learns the geometry, textures and material properties of 3D assets directly during training. Tencent says it is particularly suited to generating characters, creatures, clothing and complex props from reference artwork, preserving silhouettes and curved surfaces while producing material maps for subsequent editing.

The model compresses geometry and textures into a shared sparse representation before generating assets that match the reference image. Tencent also uses supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization to improve outputs for professional creators. Users can try the model through its Hunyuan 3D creation service, which offers five free generations per day, while developers can integrate the API into their own asset-production workflows. [IT Home, in Chinese]

item.title: Huawei plans to unveil HBM design to challenge Samsung and SK hynix
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Huawei plans to disclose a high-bandwidth memory design with twice the data-pin density of chips currently mass-produced by Samsung and SK hynix, according to a report published Thursday. The research is scheduled for presentation at a semiconductor conference in San Francisco in February. HBM supplies AI processors with the large volumes of data needed for […]
item.content:encoded:
Huawei plans to disclose a high-bandwidth memory design with twice the data-pin density of chips currently mass-produced by Samsung and SK hynix, according to a report published Thursday. The research is scheduled for presentation at a semiconductor conference in San Francisco in February.

HBM supplies AI processors with the large volumes of data needed for training and inference. Increasing the density of data connections could enable wider bandwidth between memory and processors, making the design relevant to Huawei’s broader AI-chip development. The report did not establish how close the technology is to commercial production.

Developing domestic HBM would address a major gap in China’s semiconductor supply chain. US restrictions have prevented Samsung, SK hynix and Micron from supplying HBM to Chinese customers, increasing pressure on local companies to develop alternatives as existing foreign supplies diminish. Huawei’s research extends its semiconductor work beyond processors into the memory technology needed to support them. [Bloomberg]

item.title: XREAL’s Google bet meets the holiday season
item.dc:creator: Lucia
item.description: Editor’s Note: Founded in 2017, XREAL has become a leading consumer AR-glasses maker. iResearch data cited in its Hong Kong listing application ranked it No. 1 in global AR-glasses revenue for four straight years through 2025. In October 2026, XREAL and Google launched AURA, the first wired XR glasses powered by Android XR. But can […]
item.content:encoded:
Editor’s Note: Founded in 2017, XREAL has become a leading consumer AR-glasses maker. iResearch data cited in its Hong Kong listing application ranked it No. 1 in global AR-glasses revenue for four straight years through 2025. In October 2026, XREAL and Google launched AURA, the first wired XR glasses powered by Android XR. But can the partnership turn a niche hardware business into a sustainable one?

As the holiday season gets underway, a gamer might settle onto the sofa, plug a Steam Deck into a pair of XREAL glasses, and watch its small display expand into a virtual screen. The same glasses can turn a laptop into a portable workstation or give a film its own private screen.

XREAL’s proposition spans gaming, work, and entertainment: a larger virtual screen without the need to carry a separate monitor or rely on a television.

But offering multiple use cases does not necessarily make a device part of everyday life. For XREAL, the challenge is turning occasional convenience into a lasting habit — and, ultimately, a sustainable business.

A Market Leader in a Small Pond

XREAL leads the display-based AR-glasses market, with 27% of global revenue and 24.8% of unit sales in 2025, according to iResearch data. In the broader smart-glasses market, which includes camera- and audio-focused products without displays, it ranked second by revenue. Its strength is real, but concentrated in a narrower category.

The financials show why market leadership has yet to translate into profits. Revenue climbed 30.8% in 2025 to RMB516 million, while gross margin improved to 35.2%, from 22.1% a year earlier. Even so, XREAL reported an operating loss of RMB245 million and a net loss of RMB456 million.

The net loss included a RMB203 million fair-value charge related to preferred shares, warrants, and convertible notes. The loss may indicate that higher gross margins were still insufficient to cover operating expenses.

The sales mix offers a closer look at what is driving XREAL’s growth. Its AR glasses accounted for 78.1% of 2025 revenue, while accessories contributed 14.1% and services and other income 7.8%. Within its product lineup, the One series sold about 111,000 units, compared with 17,000 for the entry-level Air series.

These figures may suggest that XREAL’s business remains largely driven by hardware sales, with services and other income making up a relatively small share of revenue. Whether software and services can become a more meaningful source of recurring income as the company expands remains an open question.

Google Adds an Ecosystem, but Demand Remains Uncertain

XREAL CEO Chi Xu has been candid about the industry’s economics. “Everybody’s losing money,” he told TechCrunch in May. He said smart glasses need three elements to come together: hardware, an operating system, and a usable interface.

For XREAL, developing these capabilities also means finding a path to profitability. Xu said the company could break even in 2027, citing plans to improve margins and reduce sales and marketing expenses.

The Google partnership is XREAL’s most prominent effort yet to strengthen its software ecosystem. Launched in October, AURA is the first wired XR glasses powered by Android XR, integrating Gemini and Google Play apps. The glasses weigh about 95 grams and connect to a separate 265-gram Compute Puck housing the processor and battery. In the US, the base model starts at $1,099 under an introductory offer, compared with its regular price of $1,279.

At that price, its initial audience may be concentrated among enthusiasts and early adopters. Broader, sustained demand will depend partly on whether its added capabilities give consumers enough reasons to use the glasses regularly.

Early reviews point to both the hardware’s potential and the software’s room for development. Engadget praised AURA’s display quality and hardware design, while noting some instability in Android XR. WIRED also highlighted its visual performance but raised questions about the hand controls and overall everyday usability.

The Google partnership gives XREAL access to a broader software ecosystem, while its hardware provides a platform for Android XR to reach consumers. Whether the combination can turn technical capabilities into a compelling everyday product remains to be seen.

For XREAL, the longer-term task is to turn its position in display glasses into a business that can support continued investment in the next generation of devices.

item.title: China launches 6G trials across eight regions, eyes 2030 rollout
item.dc:creator: Jessie Wu
item.description: China’s 6G development is finally moving from the lab into real-world industrial settings. This week, China launched a ministry-provincial collaborative pilot program for 6G innovation and development at the 2026 Global 6G Development Conference. Eight regions were selected for the first batch of trials: Beijing, Hebei, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Anhui, Hubei, and Guangdong. The launch […]
item.content:encoded:
China’s 6G development is finally moving from the lab into real-world industrial settings. This week, China launched a ministry-provincial collaborative pilot program for 6G innovation and development at the 2026 Global 6G Development Conference.

Eight regions were selected for the first batch of trials: Beijing, Hebei, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Anhui, Hubei, and Guangdong.

The launch marks another step forward in China’s 6G development. Unlike previous tests that were largely concentrated in laboratories and leading technology companies, the new program puts greater focus on connecting research with local industries and testing 6G technologies in real-world environments.

Why were these eight regions selected?

One thing worth noting is that the pilot program is not simply about rolling out 6G trials nationwide. Instead, it takes into account the industrial strengths and technological resources of different regions.

Beijing is home to a large number of research institutions and organizations involved in communications standards. Shanghai and the wider Yangtze River Delta have well-established supply chains in semiconductors and advanced manufacturing.

Guangdong has a mature ecosystem for communications devices and consumer electronics, while Hubei and Anhui have growing demand for applications in industrial manufacturing and the low-altitude economy.

The participating regions will focus on different areas, including next-generation devices, key chips and components, and satellite internet. They will also explore potential 6G applications in sectors such as the low-altitude economy, industrial manufacturing, and the marine economy.

In simple terms, each region will build on its own strengths rather than follow exactly the same development path. Bringing technology research closer to local industrial needs could help accelerate the search for commercially viable applications.

How far away is 6G commercialization?

Despite the latest progress, 6G is still several years away from commercial deployment. Globally, research into 6G remains focused on technology development, standardization, and prototype validation.

According to the current timeline set by international telecommunications organizations, the first 6G international standards are expected to take shape around 2029, with early commercial deployments potentially beginning around 2030.

China has also made considerable progress in 6G research over the past year. In 2026, the country continued to advance 6G technology trials and build up its portfolio of key technologies, with a particular focus on the 6GHz spectrum, the integration of wireless communications and AI, and satellite internet. Research is also gradually moving beyond individual technologies toward prototype equipment and system-level validation.

The new pilot program effectively brings these technologies into broader industrial environments for testing. Whether they can work reliably in real-world scenarios and deliver practical value will be a key factor in determining the industry’s next stage of development.

How is China’s 6G approach different from its 5G rollout?

Looking back at the development of 5G, the initial focus was largely on network coverage and infrastructure construction. Applications in areas such as industrial internet, autonomous driving, and cloud gaming were explored more extensively in the years that followed.

With 6G, however, the integration of communications, sensing, and AI is being emphasized from the research stage. The goal is not simply to deliver faster internet speeds, but to build networks that can sense their surroundings, connect more intelligent devices, and support complex, real-time tasks.

In the low-altitude economy, 6G could eventually help drones achieve more precise positioning, communications, and coordination. In industrial manufacturing, it could support real-time connections and collaboration among large numbers of machines. In embodied AI, more reliable, low-latency communications could also improve coordination between robots and cloud-based computing resources.

On the day the pilot program was launched, Shanghai also opened the Intelligent Connectivity Technology Research Institute, which focuses on the intersection of wireless communications and AI. Its research areas include AI-native air-interface technologies, heterogeneous general-purpose computing platforms, and systems designed for embodied AI.

These developments suggest that the future 6G race will involve much more than telecom equipment and base stations. It will also extend to semiconductors, AI, smart devices, robotics, and the broader technology ecosystem.

When will ordinary consumers be able to use 6G?

There’s no need to worry that your recently purchased 5G smartphone will become outdated anytime soon. 6G will not replace 5G overnight. Even after commercial deployment begins, building out networks, adapting devices, and developing a mature application ecosystem will take time. 5G is likely to remain the backbone of mobile communications for years to come.

For telecom equipment makers, semiconductor companies, smart device manufacturers, and robotics firms, however, now is a good time to start preparing.

After all, the opportunities created by next-generation communications may go far beyond upgrading smartphones. They could make a range of intelligent applications that are difficult to implement today commercially viable.

From the launch of pilot programs across eight regions to further technology testing and standardization, China’s 6G development is gradually moving from planning to industrial implementation.

Over the next few years, the key question will not just be how 6G networks develop, but how they integrate with AI, robotics, autonomous driving, and the low-altitude economy to create new business opportunities.

Perhaps the most exciting thing about 6G is not how much faster it can make our internet, but how many new technologies and applications it could make possible.

item.title: Tencent brings Hy4 flash to desktop computers with quantized model release
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Tencent has released GGUF quantized weights and deployment instructions for Hy4 flash, extending local use of the model to desktop computers including a 64GB Mac mini. Published through its AngelSlim model-compression project, the release includes several compression levels and support for both Apple Silicon and Nvidia hardware. The smallest listed version reduces the original model’s […]
item.content:encoded:
Tencent has released GGUF quantized weights and deployment instructions for Hy4 flash, extending local use of the model to desktop computers including a 64GB Mac mini. Published through its AngelSlim model-compression project, the release includes several compression levels and support for both Apple Silicon and Nvidia hardware.

The smallest listed version reduces the original model’s approximately 410GiB weight footprint to about 126GiB. On machines with less memory than the model’s total size, the Strata inference engine can stream expert weights from SSD storage. Tencent reports approximately 17 generated tokens per second on a 64GB M4 Pro Mac mini using that approach with an 8,000-token context.

For a 128GB M5 Max Mac, Tencent reports roughly 47 to 50 tokens per second with the Q3_K version across tested context lengths. The release also includes a vision encoder for image input and a draft model for speculative decoding, alongside setup guides for llama.cpp and Strata. [TechNode reporting]

item.title: SHEIN agrees to $100 million settlement over US shipping, reviews and customer-service claims
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: SHEIN has agreed to pay $100 million in consumer redress to settle US Federal Trade Commission allegations involving shipping promises, suppressed negative reviews, inadequate customer service and misleading supply-chain claims. The proposed settlement, announced Tuesday, requires approval by a federal judge. The FTC alleges that customers experienced lengthy delivery delays or missing purchases without adequate […]
item.content:encoded:
SHEIN has agreed to pay $100 million in consumer redress to settle US Federal Trade Commission allegations involving shipping promises, suppressed negative reviews, inadequate customer service and misleading supply-chain claims. The proposed settlement, announced Tuesday, requires approval by a federal judge.

The FTC alleges that customers experienced lengthy delivery delays or missing purchases without adequate updates, while struggling to contact support. Despite shipping nearly one million packages to the United States daily, SHEIN employed only five agents handling US telephone inquiries as of September 2025 and did not publish their phone number on its website, according to the complaint.

The regulator also alleges that SHEIN suppressed unfavorable product reviews and made unsupported claims about supplier audits and cotton origins. The proposed order would prohibit those practices and require adequate customer service. The payment would fund compensation for affected shoppers. SHEIN said in a subsequent stock-exchange announcement that the agreement does not constitute an admission of the allegations and that it disagrees with aspects of the FTC’s characterization. [TechNode reporting]

item.title: Tencent adds WeChat Music inside its messaging app
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Tencent has introduced a WeChat Music service within WeChat’s Listen feature, giving users access to music recommendations, comments and playlist-sharing functions without leaving the messaging app. The service was spotted under the personal-playlist section of Listen, accessible from WeChat’s Discover tab, according to a report published Wednesday evening. The catalog comes from QQ Music, while […]
item.content:encoded:
Tencent has introduced a WeChat Music service within WeChat’s Listen feature, giving users access to music recommendations, comments and playlist-sharing functions without leaving the messaging app. The service was spotted under the personal-playlist section of Listen, accessible from WeChat’s Discover tab, according to a report published Wednesday evening.

The catalog comes from QQ Music, while the WeChat-branded service provides its own recommendation and social features. Users can also link QQ Music or Kugou Music accounts to synchronize saved tracks and listening history. Both integrations use accounts associated with the user’s WeChat identity.

WeChat Music operates inside Listen rather than as a separate application. The setup combines music discovery and playback with the messaging platform’s existing sharing environment, while drawing on Tencent’s established music services for content and account synchronization. The report did not specify a full rollout timetable or separate pricing for the WeChat-branded service. [IT Home, in Chinese]
